sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Aṃśa** (*amsa*) — The Portion of the Sun — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Share, Portion, Light". The name means "'Portion, share' (from aṃśa), one of the twelve Ādityas"[^1].

Aṃśa is the quietest of the twelve Ādityas: the sun as the apportioner, the god whose name simply means "share." In a sacrificial universe where everything — food, merit, cattle, days — is portioned out, Aṃśa is the power that makes the portion just.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Aṃśa** and serves its temple at [aṃśa.com](https://xn--aa-2sa3170a.com). The restoration preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the anusvāra ṃ and the palatal ś — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *amsa* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.
Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam), Translated by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, 900.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **अंश**. Etymologically it means "'Portion, share' (from aṃśa), one of the twelve Ādityas"[^1].

The ASCII form *amsa* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Aṃśa** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the anusvāra ṃ and the palatal ś — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **A** — Same letter
- **m** → **ṃ** — Script-specific diacritic
- **s** → **ś** — Stress mark (acute/tone)
- **a** → **a** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **aṃśa.com** (xn--aa-2sa3170a.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɐmˈɕɐ/** — Sanskrit (IAST).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: UM-shah; the ṃ is a nasal hum, the ś a soft sh.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Devanagari** — अंश
- **Conventional** — Amsha
- **Owned form** — Aṃśa

Sanskrit aṃśa carries the anusvāra (ṃ) — a nasalization of the preceding vowel before the sibilant — written with the single dot of the Devanagari अंश. The word means "portion, share," and the restoration Aṃśa keeps the nasal exactly where the phonology and the scripture put it. The anusvāra nasalizes before the sibilant: aṃśa, never amsa — the dot is a sound, not an ornament.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **अंश**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *aṃśa*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- अ = a
- ं anusvāra = ṃ (nasal)
- श = śa
- aṃśa is one of the Ādityas, a solar portion or ray

Written अंश in Devanagari: the short a, the anusvāra dot above it, then śa. The same spelling covers the god and the common noun "share," which is precisely the theology — the Āditya is the portion, personified.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Aṃśa is the quietest of the twelve Ādityas: the sun as the apportioner, the god whose name simply means "share." In a sacrificial universe where everything — food, merit, cattle, days — is portioned out, Aṃśa is the power that makes the portion just.[^1]

### The Portion

His name is the noun: the share of sacrifice, inheritance, and fate that falls to each.

### The Twelfth Āditya

One of the twelve solar powers who rule the year's twelve portions.

### Navāṃśa

His word lives on in astrology: the navāṃśa, the ninth division of every sign.

### The Sacrifice

The fire ritual where every god receives a measured portion — his office, nightly.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Aṃśa concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The ladle** — The sruc that portions ghee into the fire — the instrument of shares
- **The lotus of the Ādityas** — Solar lineage: born of Aditi, boundless mother of the measured gods
- **The divided cake** — The sacrificial piṣṭa-paśu portioned among the gods

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Aṃśa has no single great narrative — like many Vedic gods, he is a function given face: the apportionment that the sacrifice performs and the year repeats.[^1]

### Son of Aditi (The Twelve)

The Ṛgveda knows the Ādityas as the sons of Aditi — "the unbound" — guardians of ṛta, cosmic order; the later lists count twelve, one for each month, and Aṃśa stands among them as the sun of apportionment. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa's roster names him plainly: the year itself is his household, and each month is a room of it.[^2]

### Every God a Share (The Sacrifice)

The Vedic sacrifice is an economy of portions: the hymn distributes the offering — "this share to Agni, this to Soma" — and the Brāhmaṇas explain that the gods' shares were fixed at creation. Aṃśa is the personification of that fixing: without the allotted share, no ritual holds, no inheritance stands, no year completes.

### The Gods' Shares (The Dispute)

The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa tells how the gods and anti-gods contended for the sacrifice, and how the portions were assigned — some by merit, some by trickery. The myth's lesson is the god's nature: a share is never neutral; it is the shape of justice or of theft, and Aṃśa's name sits on the scale.

### The Twelve Suns (The Year)

The Purāṇic astronomy assigns each month to one of the twelve Ādityas: the sun is one, but his offices are twelve — the creator's, the nourisher's, the portioner's — and Aṃśa's month is the year's own account rendered. The theology is exact: time itself is the oldest inheritance divided, and each month a share of the sun. His cult is the calendar: no image, no temple, only the accurate turning of the solar year, worshipped every morning in the Gāyatrī that all twelve share.

sources.citation: Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.
Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam), Translated by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, 900.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
He overlaps with Bhaga, the older "dispenser" of shares — the two are so close that Vedic lists sometimes trade their places — and with Mitra and Varuṇa, whose covenant-keeping the Ādityas collectively perform. Scholars compare the Indo-Iranian share-gods: Avestan aṃša (in Amesha Spenta, "Bounteous Immortal") is a cognate word, if a different theology — the portion raised to archangel.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], [[kali|Kālī]], and [[lakshmi|Lakṣmī]].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: His word outlived his cult: aṃśa remains the everyday Sanskrit and Hindi word for "part," and technical vocabularies are built on it — navāṃśa (the ninth harmonic chart in Jyotisha astrology), kalāṃśa in music, daśāṃśa in taxation records. Wherever Indian thought divides a whole into rightful portions — astrology, inheritance law, music theory — the god's name is the operative term.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Early Vedic religion was aniconic: no image of Aṃśa was ever made, and none was wanted — the fire altar was his only temple. The archaeology of the Ādityas is textual and structural: the śrauta fire-altars of the Śulba tradition, laid out with the geometry of portions (the altar's bricks counted and placed by rule), are the material form of his theology. Later Surya temples — Konarak, Modhera — give the solar Ādityas a collective home in stone.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

sections.label: Vedic References
sections.body:
The Āditya of portions is known by his company.

- **Āditya** — 'son of Aditi'; the family title of the twelve, the solar governors of ṛta.
- **Dvādaśa** — 'one of the Twelve'; his place in the year's solar round.
- **Bhāga-sahodara** — 'brother of Bhaga'; the pairing with the older share-god.
- **Vibhaktṛ** — 'the Apportioner'; the functional title his name translates.
- **Māsa-devatā** — 'god of the month'; the liturgical title of each Āditya in turn, his included.

sources.citation: Macdonell, Vedic Mythology (Ādityas); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.11.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Upaniṣads
sections.body: The principal Upaniṣads do not name Aṃśa — the Ādityas, like most Ṛgvedic function-gods, are absorbed there into the singular sun (āditya) as the golden Person in the disc and the eye's inner light. His office survives the abstraction: the Upanishadic sun still "apportions" the worlds and the days, and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's teaching of the sun as the world's breath keeps the Ādityan economy alive under one name. The share-god's fate is the Veda's own: the many portions gathered into the one.

sources.citation: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (sun teachings); Macdonell, Vedic Mythology.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Purāṇas
sections.body: The Purāṇas keep his name alive in the lists: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (12.11) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa enumerate the twelve Ādityas month by month, and Aṃśa stands in the roster as the sun of the apportioned year. The texts add the frame that made the Ādityas devotional: born of Aditi and Kaśyapa, they are the world's solar governors, worshipped in the twelve names at the year's twelve stations. In Purāṇic theology the portioner is no longer sacrificed to — he is bowed to, monthly, as one face of the year's single sun.

sources.citation: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.11; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.10.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Mantras & Stotras
sections.body: His mantras are the Ādityas': the **Gāyatrī** (ṚV 3.62.10) — "we meditate on the beloved light of the impeller Sun" — is addressed to the solar power all twelve share, and the **Āditya Gāyatrīs** of the later tradition give each month its own solar invocation. The sacrificial formulae of the Brāhmaṇas, which name the portions aloud ("this share to Agni, this to Soma"), are the oldest mantras of his office: the liturgy of allotment, spoken at the fire, is his worship in action.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda 3.62.10 (Gāyatrī); the Āditya Gāyatrī collections.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Aṃśa is the god of fairness at the smallest scale: not the harvest but the share; not the year but the month; not the whole but the part that is yours. He asks the oldest question of any household, any state, any life: was the portion just — and did you take only your own?

The portion-god is the least dramatic and most daily of the Ādityas, and that is his teaching: justice is mostly arithmetic — the fair share, the counted month, the inheritance divided without sleight. A sacrifice, a will, a budget, a calendar: all are his small liturgies. The sun rises each morning and apportions the day evenly to all; the rest of the work — the hymn says with characteristic bluntness — is ours.

Compare the modern ledger: double-entry bookkeeping, the census, the actuarial table — each is the share-god's craft secularized, and each fails precisely where the counting is gamed. The Vedic insight stands: a portion is a promise, and the promise is only as good as the apportioner's honesty. That is why the hymns place him among the Ādityas, the guardians of ṛta — cosmic order — rather than among the givers of boons: the share is not a gift but a right, and its measure is the oldest form of justice there is.

The year turns, the shares are counted, and the sun — the hymns repeat like a refrain — apportions the same light to all. In that daily, unglamorous fairness is the oldest image of justice India has: not the dramatic verdict, but the honest measure, renewed every morning.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
